slides.title: Logical Addressing
slides.body:
What Makes an Address "Logical"?
Every device needs a unique address at the Network Layer - one that works globally, across every network and every country. This is called a Logical Address

slides.title: Logical Addressing
slides.body:
What Makes an Address "Logical"?
The word "logical" means this address is not tied to hardware - it is assigned by the network, and it can change when the device moves to a different network

slides.title: The Five Classes of IPv4
slides.body:
Problem with Classful Addressing:
Too rigid - need 500 hosts? Class C (254) is too small, Class B (65,534) wastes 65,000+ addresses
Led to IP address exhaustion and huge routing tables
Solution → CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing)

slides.title: CIDR
slides.body:
Rules for a Valid CIDR Block
Rules for a Valid CIDR Block
Why It Exists?
Only power-of-2 blocks align with binary boundaries - any other size cannot be expressed as a single /prefix
Ensures the block starts at a clean binary boundary - routers match prefixes in binary, not decimal
A block with gaps cannot be represented by a single prefix - you would need multiple routing entries
Rule
Block size must be a power of 2
First IP must be divisible by block size
All IPs must be contiguous

slides.title: Internet Protocol - IPv4 Datagram
slides.body:
Key Fields to Remember
Header Size: Minimum 20 bytes. Maximum 60 bytes
TTL
Prevents infinite loops. Decremented at each router. Packet discarded at TTL = 0. Default: Windows = 128, Linux = 64
Protocol
Tells destination whether to hand data to TCP (6), UDP (17), or ICMP (1)

slides.title: Internet Protocol - IPv4 Datagram
slides.body:
Key Fields to Remember
Header Size: Minimum 20 bytes. Maximum 60 bytes
Fragmentation
If datagram exceeds link MTU (Ethernet = 1500 bytes), it is split. Fragments share the same Identification. MF flag = 1 for all except the last fragment. Reassembly happens only at the final destination
Header Size: Minimum 20 bytes. Maximum 60 bytes
